# Modeling of Scattering by Dense Random Media Consisting of Particle Clusters With DMRT Bicontinuous

**Jiyue Zhu**, *Member, IEEE*, **Leung Tsang**, *Life Fellow, IEEE*, and **Xiaolan Xu**, *Senior Member, IEEE*

**Abstract—In this article, we developed the dense media radiative transfer (DMRT) model for random media with densely packed particle clusters. The dense media are computer-generated by applying the bicontinuous random media characterization. The microstructure of the media is controlled by two parameters: mean grain size $\langle \zeta \rangle$ and aggregation parameter $b$. Phase matrices and extinction coefficients are computed with full-wave simulations. These are then substituted into radiative transfer (RT) equations to obtain backscattering coefficients of the dense media layer with particle clusters. The backscattering has a weaker frequency dependence (e.g., ~2.6 power for $b = 0.4$) than the Rayleigh scattering of fourth power. Backscattering results exhibit strong co-, cross-polarization (pol), and ratio of cross- to co-polarization. For applications to remote sensing of terrestrial snow at C-band, the results of DMRT simulations show that cross-polarization of snow volume scattering can be larger than that of soil surface scattering. Recently, this property of strong cross-polarization has become a useful satellite remote sensing technique for global retrieval of snow depth. Comparisons of DMRT results are made with ESA Satellite Sentinel 1 C-band data and ground-based radar observations. The calculated backscatter is in good agreement with radar measurements for both the co- and cross-polarization.**

**Index Terms—Backscattering, bicontinuous model, cross-polarization, dense media radiative transfer (DMRT), densely packed particle clusters, frequency dependence, full-wave simulation, random media, volume scattering.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

Wave propagation and scattering of random media, such as rain [1], vegetation [2], and snow [3], have been widely studied for the applications of wireless communications and remote sensing. In early studies, the Rayleigh–Gans and Mie scattering were applied to simulate the scattering of random media consisting of spherical particles [4]. For particles smaller than wavelength, Rayleigh scattering gives a frequency dependence of fourth power [5]. For dense media, wave interactions in the near field and intermediate ranges have shown different behaviors as confirmed by microwave and optical laboratory experiments, in situ measurements, and theoretical analysis [6], [7], [8]. Multiple scattering models have been proposed to compute the effective permittivity [9], [10] and scattering [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16] for dense random media. The dense media radiative transfer (DMRT) model is a method that includes wave interactions for near fields and intermediate range fields and intensity interactions for far fields. Phase matrices of densely packed spheres are computed with the quasi-crystalline approximation (QCA) in conjunction with radiative transfer (RT) forming the basis of QCA/DMRT. The QCA/DMRT models have been applied to noninteracting spheres and sticky spheres [11]. Scattering of dense medium has also been studied by the improved born approximation (IBA) [12], strong permittivity fluctuation (SPF) [13], and full-wave simulations [14], [15], [16]. These models predict small cross-polarization because of applying spherical particles [10], [11] or the use of isotropic correlation functions [14], [15], [16].

In some kinds of dense media, because particles can be densely packed, adhesive forces between particles can cause particles to form clusters or aggregates (these two terms are same). For example, terrestrial snow in mountains has large snow depth of several meters. The pressure and melt-freeze events can make ice grains in snow to adhere to form ice clusters (ice aggregates) [17], [18]. Unlike spherical grains [11], ice clusters in snow have irregular shapes. The irregular shapes of clusters are one possible reason to cause stronger scattering for cross-pol. Those clusters also increase the ratio of cross- to co-pol. Scattering by ice aggregates has been studied in the past for cloud and precipitation at microwave and optical frequencies [19], [20]. However, ice aggregates in the atmosphere have sparse concentration, so that scattering by aggregates can be calculated by adding intensities from different aggregates. For aggregates that are densely packed, a wave approach needs to be used to account for wave interactions among the aggregates within near and intermediate distances (up to three wavelengths). Previous DMRT models have not considered the effects of dense aggregates [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16].

**Fig. 1.** Radar backscattering from a layer of random medium in DMRT. The cubic sample volumes of size $L$ are used to simulate the phase matrices of random media, which are next used in RT equations.

A motivation of this article is that Lievens et al. [17] showed the ability of European Space Agency (ESA) satellite Sentinel-1 C-band radar data to map snow depth in the Northern Hemisphere mountains. The data show that C-band cross-pol radar backscatter increases with snow depth. The results are surprising because C-band snow volume scattering was trusted to be negligible due to the wavelength of C-band (5.4 GHz) is 5.5 cm, which is 50 times larger than ice grain size in snow which is in the order of 1 mm [5], [21]. It was believed that snow volume scattering at C-band is much smaller than surface scattering of the underlying rough snow/soil interface (see Fig. 1) [21]. The results of Lievens et al. [17] have aroused great interests because they indicate the new possibility of using cross-pol of C-band radar data to monitor global snow depth in mountainous regions [17]. However, physical reasons causing strong cross-pol are still unclear for the snow community. It may be caused by the anisotropy of ice particles, ice clusters, or inhomogeneities in the snowpack. Multiple scattering is also one of the reasons, but, based on multiple scattering only, cross-pol signals predicted by the DMRT model are still weaker than measured data.

In this article, we have two novel contributions. One is that this article investigates the effects of clustered ice grains within snow (one possible reason) on scattering at cross-pol for C-band and up to Ku-band (17 GHz). So far, there are no literatures published to theoretically study the multiple scattering of snow at C-band [17]. The other is that this article improves the bicontinuous model [3], [14], [15], [16] to make it capable for the modeling of dense ice clusters in snow. In this article, we apply the DMRT model for multiple scattering of random media. Fig. 1 illustrates the essence of DMRT for dense media, which consists of a coherent step followed by an incoherent step. In the first coherent step, we solve Maxwell equations within a volume of dense particle clusters of several wavelengths, so that the wave interactions in the near field and intermediate field range are accounted. Using the results of full-wave simulations, the effective scattering coefficients, extinction coefficients, and phase matrix are calculated. In the second incoherent step, these quantities are then substituted into the RT equations, which account for far-field incoherent intensity interactions within the layer and between layers. The RT equations are then solved to calculate the backscattering.

To represent the microstructure of dense particle clusters, the bicontinuous random media [3], [14], [15], [16] has been improved. The clusters are quantified by correlation function and spectral density. The correlation function $C(\bar{r})$ gives statistical correlation of two random variables. Specifically, for statistically homogenous random media, $C(\bar{r}) = C(\bar{r}_1 - \bar{r}_2) = \langle \Theta(\bar{r}_1)\Theta(\bar{r}_2) \rangle$, where $\Theta(\bar{r})$ is the random distribution of the media. The spectral density $W(k)$ is the 3-D Fourier transform of the correlation function [3], [5]

$$ W(k) = 4\pi \int_0^{\infty} dr r^2 \frac{\sin(kr)}{kr} C_\Theta(r) \quad (1) $$

where $k$ is the medium wavenumber.

The DMRT simulations in this article show that dense clusters enhance volume scattering for co- and cross-pol and for cross-/co-pol ratio. The frequency dependence of scattering of dense clusters is reduced (with $b = 0.4$, to ~2.6 power) from 5 to 17 GHz (C- to Ku-band), which is consistent with our recent symposium paper [22] and the dissertation of Zhu [23]. For a thin layer, surface scattering of rough interface is larger than volume scattering. However, volume scattering of aggregates increases with layer thickness. The volume scattering at cross-pol can surpass the magnitude of surface scattering. Simulation results are also compared against radar observations from Sentinel 1 data [17] and ground-based experiments [24] for both co- and cross-pol.

The organization of this article is as follows. In Section II, the bicontinuous random media is used for generating random media with dense aggregates. The correlation function and spectral density of the bicontinuous medium are illustrated and used to quantify dense aggregates. In Section III, we summarize the methodology and equations of DMRT. In Section IV, the various convergences of Monte Carlo simulations are carried out. Backscattering simulation results are compared with satellite and ground measurements.

## II. CHARACTERIZATION OF BICONTINUOUS RANDOM MEDIA WITH DENSE AGGREGATES

The microstructure of random media with densely packed aggregates is represented by the bicontinuous random media [3]. We consider the case of a two-phase random medium that consists of particles and background. For the case of terrestrial snow, the background is air and the particles are ice with a relative permittivity of 3.2. In the bicontinuous media, the microstructure of aggregates is controlled by two parameters: mean grain size $\langle \zeta \rangle$ and aggregation parameter $b$. The smaller $b$ is, the larger are the aggregates. The computer generation procedure is as follows [3]. A random function of position $S(\bar{r})$ is generated by the formula

$$ S(\bar{r}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \cos(\bar{\zeta}_n \cdot \bar{r} + \phi_n) \quad (2) $$

where $N$ is a large integer (e.g., $N = 10^4$) to satisfy the central limit theorem, and $\bar{\zeta}_n$ is a random wave vector $\bar{\zeta}_n = \zeta_n \hat{\zeta}_n$. The unit vector $\hat{\zeta}_n$ is uniformly distributed on a unit spherical surface. The phase $\phi_n$ is a random variable uniformly distributed between 0 and $2\pi$. The magnitude $\zeta_n$ of $\bar{\zeta}_n$ is a random variable, which is between 0 and $\infty$. In previous studies [3], [14], [15], the gamma distribution was used for the probability density function (pdf), $p(\zeta_n)$. There are two parameters, $\langle \zeta \rangle$ and $b$, in gamma distribution [3]. $\langle \zeta \rangle$ is the mean value of $\zeta_n$, which is inversely proportional to grain size with a unit of m$^{-1}$. $b$ is a dimensionless aggregation parameter and inversely related to the standard deviation of $\zeta_n$. The correlation functions and spectral densities are calculated in [3] and [22]. The spectral density is related to the scattering properties.

The previous bicontinuous media characterization [3] is not able to model dense aggregates. To generate dense aggregates, parameter $b$ should be less than 1. With a fixed $\langle \zeta \rangle$ and $b < 1$, the issue is that the spectral density $W(k)$ does not converge at low wavenumber causing nonconvergent scattering results. As indicated by (1), considering low wavenumber ($k \to 0$), $(\sin(kr))/kr \to 1$. Then $W(k) \sim \int_0^{\infty} r^2 C_\Theta(r) dr$. To get well-converged $W(k)$, the normalized covariance $C_\Theta(r)$ of the random media should decay faster than $(1/r^3)$. However, $C_\Theta(r)$ of the previous characterization gives decay slower than $(1/r^3)$. Given certain $\langle \zeta \rangle$ and $b$, the only thing that can be changed to get a fast decay $C_\Theta(r)$ is $p(\zeta)$. For the previous $p(\zeta)$ [3], when $\zeta$ approaches zero, $p(\zeta)$ is approximately proportional to $(\zeta/\langle \zeta \rangle)^b$ and decays slowly (see Fig. 2). To solve this problem, $p(\zeta)$ is adjusted to make it decay faster near zero. The tuned $p(\zeta)$ is

$$ p(\zeta) = \begin{cases} a \exp\left(-\dfrac{\zeta_j}{\zeta}\right), & \text{for } \zeta \le \zeta_j \\ \dfrac{(b+1)^{b+1}}{\Gamma(b+1)\langle \zeta \rangle} \left(\dfrac{\zeta}{\langle \zeta \rangle}\right)^b \exp\left(-(b+1)\dfrac{\zeta}{\langle \zeta \rangle}\right), & \text{for } \zeta > \zeta_j. \end{cases} \quad (3) $$

In (3), the gamma distribution is truncated at $\zeta_j$ and replaced by an exponential function that has an argument inversely proportional to $\zeta$. The coefficient $a$ is determined by normalization of the pdf, $\int_0^{\infty} d\zeta p(\zeta) = 1$. In Fig. 2, the tuned $p(\zeta)$ has much faster decay near zero than the gamma distribution. For gamma distribution with $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$ and $b = 0.4$, the standard deviation is $9296.69 \text{ m}^{-1}$. For tuned $p(\zeta)$ with $\zeta_j = 150 \text{ m}^{-1}$ and $b = 0.4$, $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000.1 \text{ m}^{-1}$ and the standard deviation is $9296.61 \text{ m}^{-1}$. The tuned $p(\zeta)$ has almost the same standard deviation as the previous $p(\zeta)$ but has good convergence property for the spectral density.

**Fig. 2.** Comparison of the pdf of $\zeta_n$ between the gamma distribution and the tuned gamma distribution for $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$, $b = 0.4$, and the truncated $\zeta_j = 150 \text{ m}^{-1}$.

In computer generation, for every position $\bar{r}$ within the medium, an indicator function is defined as

$$ \Theta(\bar{r}) = \begin{cases} 1, & S(\bar{r}) > \alpha \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (4) $$

where $\alpha$ is a threshold and related to the volume fraction occupied by the particles $f_v$, $f_v = (1/2)[1 - \text{erf}(\alpha)] = \langle \Theta(\bar{r}) \rangle$. For a position $\bar{r}$, if the indicator $\Theta(\bar{r}) = 0$, the point is in the background medium. Otherwise, the point $\bar{r}$ is in a particle. Using (2)–(4) samples of bicontinuous media with dense aggregates is generated.

The bicontinuous correlation function of $\Theta(\bar{r})$ is given as [3]

$$ C_\Theta(\bar{r}) = f_v^2 + \sum_{m=1}^{+\infty} C_m(\alpha)[C_S(r)]^m \quad (5) $$

where $C_m(\alpha) = ((\exp(-2\alpha^2)H_{m-1}^2(\alpha))/(\pi m! 2^m))$ and $H_{m-1}(\alpha)$ is the Hermite polynomial. $C_S(r) = \int_0^{\infty} d\zeta p(\zeta)((\sin(\zeta r))/\zeta r)$ is the normalized correlation function of $S(\bar{r})$. The covariance of the bicontinuous medium is $C_\Theta(r) = \Gamma(\bar{r}) - f_v^2$.

**Fig. 3.** (a) Normalized covariance and (b) spectral density for original and tuned bicontinuous medium with $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$ and $b = 0.4$.

In Fig. 3, the normalized covariance and spectral density for the previous $p(\zeta)$ and tuned $p(\zeta)$ are illustrated. The normalized covariance of the tuned $p(\zeta)$ is the same for short distance (<10 mm) but has large decay in larger distance. For $\zeta_j > 150 \text{ m}^{-1}$, the spectral density is similar at high spectrum (>250 rad/m) and becomes smaller for low spectrum. In the tuned characterization, $\zeta_j$ is chosen, so that we have uniform spectral density within the spectrum range for microwave frequencies between 5 and 19 GHz. In Fig. 4, we compare the normalized covariance and spectral density for the tuned characterization with different $b$ parameters and $\zeta_j = 150 \text{ m}^{-1}$. The correlation function $C_\Theta(r)$ has a larger tail for smaller $b$, which indicates strong aggregation for the media. The spectral density $W(k)$ has a steeper slope for smaller $b$. This causes stronger scattering and weaker frequency dependence.

**Fig. 4.** (a) Normalized covariance and (b) spectral density for the tuned bicontinuous medium for different aggregation with $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$.

**Fig. 5.** Illustration of media microstructure represented by the tuned bicontinuous medium. White are particles and black are background. The microstructure of the random media has volume fraction $f_v = 0.3$ and 1 mm mean grain size ($\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$) (a) with dense aggregates $b = 0.4$ and (b) without aggregates $b = 2.0$.

We compare the microstructure of the bicontinuous medium with dense aggregates [see Fig. 5(a)] and without aggregates [see Fig. 5(b)]. Both figures have the same mean grain size of 1 mm but different aggregation properties. Particles in Fig. 5(a) are packed to form large aggregates, while particles in Fig. 5(b) are randomly distributed without the features of aggregation. The pictures correspond with the covariance shown in Fig. 4. In this article, the default chosen microstructure parameters are $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$ and $b = 0.4$, corresponding with $a = 1.4007 \times 10^{-4}$ for $\zeta_j = 150 \text{ m}^{-1}$.

## III. DMRT WITH FULL-WAVE SIMULATION FOR DENSELY PACKED AGGREGATES

The DMRT model is as indicated in Fig. 1. The first step is to apply the full-wave simulations to computer the scattering coefficient, extinction coefficient, and phase matrix of dense aggregates samples with sample sizes of several wavelengths. The sample volumes used are cubes and slabs. The second step is to solve RT equations with calculated phase matrices to obtain the backscattering coefficient of a layer of dense aggregates.

### A. Step 1: Full-Wave Simulations for Dense Aggregates

For the bicontinuous random medium, the spatial distribution of the relative permittivity is expressed as

$$ \varepsilon_r(\bar{r}) = (\varepsilon_p - 1)\Theta(\bar{r}) + 1 \quad (6) $$

where $\varepsilon_p$ is the relative permittivity of particles and $\Theta(\bar{r})$ is the indicator function given in (4). Consider a sample volume $V$ of dense aggregates. Let an incident plane wave in $\hat{k}_i$ direction with polarization $\hat{e}_i$ giving $\bar{E}^{inc} = \hat{e}_i \exp(i\bar{k}_i \cdot \bar{r})$, where $\bar{k}_i = k\hat{k}_i$, $k$ is the free space wavenumber. The scattered field from the sample volume is

$$ \bar{E}_s(\bar{r}) = k^2 \int_V d\bar{r}' \bar{\bar{G}}_0(\bar{r}, \bar{r}') \cdot (\varepsilon_r(\bar{r}') - 1)\bar{E}(\bar{r}') \quad (7) $$

where $\bar{\bar{G}}_0(\bar{r}, \bar{r}')$ is the free space dyadic Green function. The scattered field in the far field of the sample volume is [3], using the 1-2 polarization system

$$ \bar{E}_s(\bar{r}) = \frac{k^2 \exp(ikr)}{4\pi r} (\varepsilon_p - 1)(\hat{1}_s\hat{1}_s + \hat{2}_s\hat{2}_s) \cdot \int_V d\bar{r}' \exp(-ik\hat{k}_s \cdot \bar{r}') \Theta(\bar{r}') \bar{E}(\bar{r}') \quad (8) $$

where $\hat{k}_s$ is the observation direction. In the 1-2 frame, $\hat{1}_s = \hat{1}_i = ((\hat{k}_s \times \hat{k}_i)/(|\hat{k}_s \times \hat{k}_i|))$, $\hat{2}_s = \hat{k}_s \times \hat{1}_s$, and $\hat{2}_i = \hat{k}_i \times \hat{1}_i$. Thus, the polarization of incident waves can be expressed as $\hat{e}_i = \hat{1}_i(\hat{1}_i \cdot \hat{e}_i) + \hat{2}_i(\hat{2}_i \cdot \hat{e}_i)$. The observation angle is such that $cos\theta_s = \hat{k}_s \cdot \hat{k}_i$.

*1) Numerical Method for the Scattered Field Computation:* We use discrete-dipole approximation (DDA) to solve (7) [3], [14], [15], [16]. In DDA, the sample volume $V$ is discretized into small cubes, assuming $M$ is the total number of particle cubes and the volume of the particle cube is $\Delta V = d^3$, where $d$ is the side length. Then, (7) in discretized format [3], [14], is

$$ \bar{p}_i = \alpha_i \bar{E}^{inc}_i + \alpha_i \sum_{j=1, j\neq i}^{M} \frac{k^2}{\varepsilon} \bar{\bar{G}}_0(\bar{r}_i, \bar{r}_j) \cdot \bar{p}_j \quad (9) $$

where $\bar{p}_i = \Delta V (\varepsilon_p - 1)\varepsilon \bar{E}_i$ is the dipole moment of the $i$th ice cube and $\bar{E}^{inc}_i$, $\bar{E}_i$, and $\alpha_i$ are the values of the incident field, the internal field, and the polarizability in the $i$th particle cube, respectively. The polarizability $\alpha_i$ is given [3], [14]

$$ \alpha_i = \frac{\alpha_i^C}{1 - \frac{\alpha_i^C}{4\pi\varepsilon d^3} [(\frac{4\pi}{3})^{1/3}k^2 d^2 + \frac{2ik^3 d^3}{3}]} \quad (10) $$

where $\alpha_i^C = 3\varepsilon d^3 [(\varepsilon_p - 1)/(\varepsilon_p + 2)]$, and $\varepsilon$ is the free space permittivity. Multiple random media sample volumes (realizations) are generated. For each realization, (9) are solved, and then, (8) is used to calculate scattered far field of the sample.

*2) Coherent and Incoherent Field Decomposition:* Using Monte Carlo simulations, realizations averaging is used to obtain the coherent and incoherent field. The coherent field is obtained by averaging the scattered field [3], [5]

$$ \bar{E}_s^{coh} = \langle \bar{E}_s \rangle = \frac{1}{N_r} \sum_{p=1}^{N_r} \bar{E}_s^p \quad (11) $$

where $N_r$ is the number of realizations and $p$ is the index of realizations, $p = 1, 2, ..., N_r$. The incoherent field is obtained by subtracting the coherent field for each realization [3], [5]

$$ \bar{E}_s^{inco,p} = \bar{E}_s^p - \langle \bar{E}_s \rangle. \quad (12) $$

*3) Phase Matrix, Scattering Coefficients, and Extinction Coefficients:* The coherent and incoherent bistatic scattering cross sections are, respectively, the coherent and incoherent scattered wave intensities normalized by the incident wave intensity [3], [5]

$$ \sigma_{coh}(\hat{k}_s, \hat{k}_i) = \frac{r^2 |\langle \bar{E}_s \rangle|^2}{|\bar{E}^{inc}|^2} \quad (13) $$

$$ \sigma_{inco}(\hat{k}_s, \hat{k}_i) = \frac{r^2}{|\bar{E}^{inc}|^2} \frac{1}{N_r} \sum_{p=1}^{N_r} |\bar{E}_s^{inco,p}|^2. \quad (14) $$

The phase matrix $P(\hat{k}_s, \hat{k}_i)$ is the bistatic scattering cross section $\sigma(\hat{k}_s, \hat{k}_i)$ per unit volume [3], [5]

$$ P(\hat{k}_s, \hat{k}_i) = \frac{\sigma(\hat{k}_s, \hat{k}_i)}{V}. \quad (15) $$

The incoherent phase matrix is used in the RT equations [14], [15], [16]. The scattering coefficient $\kappa_s$ is obtained by integrating the incoherent bistatic scattering cross section over the solid angle $4\pi$ and then normalized by the sample volume [3], [5]

$$ \kappa_s = \frac{2\pi}{V} \int_0^{\pi} d\theta_s \sin\theta_s \sigma_{inco}(\hat{k}_s, \hat{k}_i). \quad (16) $$

The extinction coefficient is the sum of the absorption coefficient and the scattering coefficient, $\kappa_e = \kappa_s + \kappa_a$. The absorption coefficient $\kappa_a$ is computed from the internal field of cubes of particles in DDA [5].

### B. Step 2: RT Equations for Backscattering of a Layer of Dense Aggregates

The second step in DMRT is to calculate the backscattering of dense aggregates layers (see Fig. 1). The calculated phase matrix, scattering coefficient, and extinction coefficient calculated in step 1 from sample volumes are substituted into the RT equations [5], [14], [15], [16]

$$ \frac{d\bar{I}(\bar{r}, \hat{s})}{ds} = -\kappa_e \bar{I}(\bar{r}, \hat{s}) + \int_{4\pi} d\Omega' \bar{\bar{P}}(\bar{r}, \hat{s}, \hat{s}') \cdot \bar{I}(\bar{r}, \hat{s}') \quad (17) $$

where $\bar{I}(\bar{r}, \hat{s})$ is the specific intensity at the position $\bar{r}$ in direction $\hat{s}$ inside the random media. The RT equations are solved by the eigen-quadrature approach [15]. Simulations given in this article consider a single uniform medium layer. For random media with multiple layers, the proposed model is also applicable. Phase matrix and scattering properties are computed for each layer as step 1. Then, substitute them into the RT equations to calculate total backscatter of all the layers [15].

## IV. NUMERICAL RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

In this section, we illustrate numerical results for step 1 and step 2 of the DMRT models. We also compare model results with the ESA satellite Sentinel 1 data [17] and ground-based radar observations [24]. The default media parameters are volume fraction $f_v = 0.3$ and $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$, which is equal to a grain size of 1 mm. The background medium is air and the particle permittivity is $\varepsilon_p = 3.2$, which is the permittivity of pure ice. The frequency range is from 5 to 19 GHz, which covers 5.4 GHz (Sentinel 1 satellite), 9.6 GHz (TerraSAR X satellite and COSMO-SkyMed satellite), 13.3 GHz (QuickScat satellite), and 17.2 GHz (SnowSAR, airborne instrument).

**Fig. 6.** Convergences of realizations and discretization: phase matrices in decibel for both co- and cross-pol at 5.4 GHz for the random medium with $f_v = 0.3$, $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$ and $b = 0.4$. The sample cube is 6.4 cm. Tests are for (a) different numbers of realizations with discretization of 0.5 mm and (b) different discretization sizes with 100 realizations.

**Fig. 7.** Convergences of sample sizes and sample shapes: phase matrices in decibel for both co- and cross-pol at 5.4 GHz with respect to the simulation size for the random medium with $f_v = 0.3$, $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$ and $b = 0.4$. The number of realization is 100 and the discretization of 0.5 mm. Tests are for (a) sample size with 6.4 cm and 9.4 cube and (b) sample shape with 6.4 cm cube and $12 \times 12 \times 6.4$ cm slab.

### A. Results of Step 1: Phase Matrix and Scattering Coefficient

*1) Statistical and Computation Convergence Test:* We conduct four kinds of convergence tests with respect to numerical parameters: the number of realizations, the discretization in DDA, and the simulation sample size and shape. We show the convergence for $P_{11}$ and $P_{21}$. Convergence tests for $P_{22}$ and $P_{12}$ are similar.

In Fig. 6(a), the convergence with the number of realization is illustrated. The phase matrices for both polarizations with 50 and 100 realizations are plotted. Results show only small variations for phase matrices with respect to the number of realizations. The convergence with the DDA discretization size is shown in Fig. 6(b). The grain size is 1 mm, which is less than 1/55 wavelength for the frequency of 5.4 GHz. The DDA discretization size needs to be small enough to describe the microstructure of the bicontinuous medium. Comparing the results with discretization size of 0.25 and 0.5 mm, both $P_{11}$ and $P_{21}$ are in good agreement for two kinds of discretization. In random medium simulations, for a cube of 6.4 cm, the number of ice particles is approximately $7.864 \times 10^4$, so that there are enough number of particles to simulate random media scattering inside the sample cube.

In Fig. 7(a), the phase matrices of sample cubes with two different sample sizes of 6.4 and 9.6 cm are shown. The results show agreement for both polarizations. $P_{21}$ of the sample cube of 9.6 cm is slightly stronger than that of 6.4 cm. In Fig. 7(b), the phase matrices of $12 \times 12 \times 6.4$ cm sample slab and 6.4 cm sample cube are compared for both co- and cross-pol. The phase matrices of the sample slab are in good agreement with those of the sample cube. Compared with the results of the 6.4 cm sample cube, the 9.6 cm sample cube and the sample slab results have some fluctuations because of the larger size. Also, more variations appear in cross-pol results. In general, good convergence is achieved in the two tests.

*2) Phase Matrix and Scattering Coefficients of Dense Aggregates:* We next simulate phase matrices and scattering coefficients. For this part, the DDA discretization is 0.5 mm, the sample is chosen as $12 \times 12 \times 6.4$ cm slab, and the number of realizations is larger than 50.

In Fig. 8, the phase matrix of a sample slab with different aggregation is compared at 5.4 and 17.2 GHz for both co- and cross-pol. In general, scattering increases with the aggregation level ($b$ decreases). With more aggregation, the diameter and number of aggregates increase, giving stronger scattering. When $b$ is reduced from 0.8 to 0.4, the scattering power increases about 3–5 dB at 17.2 GHz and 5–7 dB at 5.4 GHz. Furthermore, the scattering coefficient of $b = 0.4$ at 17.2 GHz is about 2.5 times of $b = 0.8$, while it is 3.5 times at 5.4 GHz. These indicate that the effects of dense aggregates have more impact at lower frequency giving weaker frequency dependence.

**Fig. 8.** Comparison of the incoherent phase matrices in decibel of a dense aggregates sample slab ($12 \times 12 \times 6.4$ cm) from DDA simulations for both co- and cross-pol with different aggregation at (a) 17.2 and (b) 5.4 GHz. The microstructure parameters are $f_v = 0.3$ and $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$.

**Fig. 9.** Frequency dependence of scattering coefficients for random media with different aggregation from 5 to 19 GHz. The snow parameters are $f_v = 0.3$ and $\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$.

The frequency dependence of scattering coefficients from 5 to 19 GHz is illustrated in Fig. 9. In general, with $b = 0.4$ and 0.8, the frequency dependence is ~2.6 and ~3.3 power, respectively, weaker than the fourth power of Rayleigh scattering. For $b = 2.0$, the frequency dependence is ~3.9 power close to that of Rayleigh scattering. $b = 2.0$ indicates that there is no aggregation. The frequency dependence for $b = 0.4$ is weaker than that of $b = 0.8$ and the scattering coefficients are larger due to stronger scattering caused by more aggregation.

### B. Results of Step 2: Backscattering of a Layer of Random Media Consisting of Dense Aggregates

*1) Scattering by a Layer of Random Medium:* We calculate backscattering of a layer of media with dense aggregates at C-band (5.4 GHz). The interface of the bottom dielectric and random media is rough. The total backscattering is composed by two parts: volume scattering component from dense aggregates and rough surface scattering component [14]. We take into account the attenuation of the random media layer when considering the surface scattering. Full-wave simulations of dielectric rough surface have been limited to 1/4 of a medium wavelength. For random media with an effective dielectric constant of 1.5, 1/4 of a wavelength at C-band means $5.5/(4\sqrt{1.5}) = 1.1$ cm, which is smaller than most of the rough soil surfaces. The Oh model used regression curve fitting based on field measurements of four values of rms heights [25]. The amount of data is limited, yet it is used because it extends beyond the usual height of quarter wavelength. We use the Oh model for the surface scattering.

We simulate the volume scattering of the dense aggregates layer as a function of frequency with a thickness of 1.2 m and a particle size of 1 mm. Two cases are considered: $b = 0.4$ with dense aggregates and $b = 2.0$ without aggregates. Results are illustrated in Fig. 10. The volume scattering of dense aggregates is stronger than that of media without aggregates case for both polarizations. The difference at cross-pol is larger than co-pol. The dense aggregates enhance the volume scattering for both polarizations.

For the dense aggregates layer, the cross- to co-pol ratio of volume scattering is larger than that of rough surface scattering. Thus, although co-pol volume scattering is less than that of surface scattering, the cross-pol volume scattering can exceed that of surface scattering. In Fig. 11, we compare volume scattering with surface scattering at 5.4 GHz with respect to thickness. The soil surface has a permittivity of $9 + 2.5i$ and an rms height of 1.5 cm. The surface scattering has a small attenuation by the dense aggregates layer. The surface scattering of co-pol is about -10 dB and the cross-pol is about -20 dB. Volume scattering of dense aggregates ($b = 0.4$) increases with thickness. Note that, for co-pol, surface scattering is larger than volume scattering until about 160 cm thickness. For cross-pol, volume scattering can be larger than surface scattering for large thickness (above 1 m in the example).

**Fig. 10.** Backscattering coefficients for a layer of random media with dense aggregates ($b = 0.4$) and without aggregates ($b = 2.0$) from 5 to 19 GHz. The layer thickness is 1.2 m, volume fraction is $f_v = 0.3$, and particle size is about 1 mm ($\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$). The permittivity of particle is $\varepsilon_p = 3.2$ and background is air.

**Fig. 11.** (a) Surface scattering and (b) volume scattering as a function of thickness for a layer of dense aggregates at 5.4 GHz. The random medium has volume fraction $f_v = 0.3$, particle size is about 1 mm ($\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$), and aggregation parameter $b = 0.4$. The permittivity of particle is $\varepsilon_p = 3.2$ and background is air. The bottom dielectric surface has a permittivity of $\varepsilon_g = 9.0 + 2.5i$ and an rms height of 1.5 cm.

*2) Applications for Snow Remote Sensing: Snowpack With Dense Ice Particle Aggregates:* We next apply the DMRT model to a single snow layer over soil with a rough snow/soil interface. In the past, the DMRT models were applied to higher frequencies, such as X- and Ku-bands, because of stronger volume scattering than surface scattering [14], [15], [16]. As indicated by the Sentinel 1 data [17] and ground-based radar measurements [24], the backscattering of cross-pol at C-band can increase with snow accumulation. The numerical results shown in this article indicate that dense ice aggregates in snowpack can enhance the volume scattering for both co- and cross-pol.

We apply the C- and X-band radar measurements collected by Kendra et al. [24] during February 1993. For measurements in [24], the snowpack is not naturally formed but artificially generated. The artificial snow was accumulated and spread into a uniform layer. Thus, the snowpack is isotropic and easy to be well-characterized by measurements. The measured ground and snow conditions are listed in Table I. In Kendra et al.’s [24] study, the RT theory with Rayleigh scattering was applied to fit with measurements. The grain size used for X-band was 0.9 mm, while for C-band was 1.7 mm, much larger than the in situ measurements. The possible missing point here is the effects of aggregates. We generate the snowpack with aggregates using measured physical parameters in Table I. The surface scattering is calculated by the Oh model [25] (the same model as Kendra did). The phase matrix of the snow slab is simulated by DDA with discretization of 0.25 mm and 50 realizations. The simulated backscattering coefficient is the sum of volume scattering from the DMRT and surface scattering [14], [15] (see Fig. 12). Compared with the measurements data, both C- and X-band backscattering are in good agreement with radar measurements for both co- and cross-pol. The cross-pol backscattering of X-band is about 2 dB larger than radar data in incident angles of $20^{\circ}$–$50^{\circ}$. This example does show by including aggregate effects, and the DMRT model results are in good agreement C-band radar data for both co- and cross-pol.

**TABLE I**
**SNOW AND GROUND PROPERTIES FOR BACKSCATTERING SIMULATIONS OF FIG. 12**

| Ground | Snow microstructure | Snow depth |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| rms height = 0.37 cm | grain size = 0.275mm | |
| $\varepsilon_{r,g} = 4.6 + 0.5i$ | $\langle \zeta \rangle = 40000 \text{ m}^{-1}$ | Snow depth=60cm |
| | $b = 0.4, f_v = 0.5234$ | |

**Fig. 12.** Comparison of simulated backscattering coefficients from the DMRT model with radar measurements based on the study by Kendra et al. [24]. (a) C-band and (b) X-band results.

Next, we compare the DMRT simulations with Sentinel 1 data (5.4 GHz) data taken in the winter of 2018. The data are reported in [17]. In this example, soil surface scattering is obtained by radar observations before the snow accumulation (-8.5 dB for VV and -16 dB for VH). We assume that the soil condition is constant during the winter season. For parameters of snowpack, only snow depth measurements are available [17]. There are no other in situ measurements, such as snow density, snow grain size, and specific surface area (SSA). In this simulation, we assume dry snow and give a guess for other absent parameters: volume fraction $f_v = 0.3$, grain size about 1 mm ($\langle \zeta \rangle = 11000 \text{ m}^{-1}$), and aggregation parameter $b = 0.4$. Also, these guessed snow parameters are assumed to be constant during the dry snow season. The comparisons of simulated backscatter and radar observations are plotted in Fig. 13. The simulated results are in good agreement with the satellite data for both polarizations. Note that the co-pol radar data fluctuate around -8 dB, showing no sensitivity to snow depth. However, cross-pol backscatter increases with snow depth by about 2 dB, showing sensitivity to snow depth. As indicated in Fig. 13 and Lievens’s study [17], cross-pol signal have small variations (<0.5 dB) for snowpack with depth below 0.5 m. Thus, C-band radar is applicable for the detection of snow with depth above 1 m. For snowpack less than 1 m, other higher bands (X and Ku) are more suitable since volume scattering is more significant at higher frequencies [14], [15], [16].

**Fig. 13.** Comparison of simulated backscattering coefficients from the DMRT model with Sentinel 1 data from the study by Lievens et al. [17]. Snow depth measurements are from the interactive multisensor snow and ice mapping system (IMS) [17]. Site details, including mountain range and latitude/longitude/elevation: Omineca Mountains, BC, Canada ($57.53^{\circ}\text{N}/-126.73^{\circ}\text{E}/1331$ m).

## V. CONCLUSION

We have developed a DMRT model for the scattering of random media with dense aggregates. Full-wave simulations are used to derive the phase matrix of dense aggregates. Multiple scattering of a layer of dense aggregates is calculated by the RT equations. We have improved the bicontinuous random media characterization to model dense aggregates. We investigated the frequency and polarization dependence of scattering of dense aggregates from 5 to 19 GHz. Results show that dense aggregates can cause stronger than expected volume scattering for both co- and cross-pol. The results of the DMRT model are in good agreement with the spaceborne and ground-based radar measurements. In the model, the physical size of aggregates depends on ice grain size and parameter $b$. With $b$ changing from 2.0 to 0.4, frequency dependence is reduced from 3.9 to 2.58 and cross-pol backscatter at C-band increases 25 dB for the example in Fig. 10. This indicates that cross-pol is sensitive to size variations of aggregates.

Although the model has been applied to backscatter of terrestrial snow (see Fig. 10) and validated with radar measurements (see Figs. 12 and 13), there are facts that have not been considered in this article. As mentioned in [17], the anisotropic snow structure is another important element, which contributes to cross polarization but not affect much co-pol. Surface scattering from interfaces of layers within snow can also be the possibility. Simulation of Fig. 13 only shows that the model can predict reasonable co- and cross-pol backscatter, but issues also exist. Not only the parameter $b$ used in this article is assumed, which is not from in situ measurements, but also snow anisotropy and inhomogeneities are not considered. For future studies, we need to have radar data with in situ measurements to support the model validation. We also need to study anisotropic snow by incorporating the study of [26] and the effects of inhomogeneities on cross-pol.

**Jiyue Zhu** (Member, IEEE) received the B.E. degree in electrics and information engineering from Xidian University, Xi’an, China, in 2012, the M.Sc. degree in electromagnetics and microwave techniques from Southeast University, Nanjing, China, in 2015, and the Ph.D. degree in electric engineering from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA, in 2021.
His research interests include wave propagation and scattering for random rough surface and random media, and computational electromagnetics in remote sensing for soil moisture and snow.

**Leung Tsang** (Life Fellow, IEEE) was born in Hong Kong. He received the B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. degrees in electrical engineering and computer science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA, in 1971, 1973, and 1976, respectively.
He was a Professor of electrical engineering with the University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA, from 1983 to 2014. He was the Chair of the Department from 2006 to 2011. From 2001 to 2004, he was on leave from the University of Washington and he was also at the City University of Hong Kong. He is currently a Professor with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA. His current research interests include waves in random media and rough surfaces, remote sensing, computational electromagnetics, signal integrity, and optics.
Dr. Tsang is a fellow of the Optical Society of America. He received the IEEE Third Millennium Medal in 2000; the Outstanding Service Award from the IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Society in 2000; the Distinguished Achievement Award from the IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Society in 2008; the Fiorino Oro Award from the CeTeM, Italy, in 2010; the William Pecora Award co-sponsored by the U.S. Department of Interior and NASA in 2012; and the 2013 IEEE Electromagnetics Award. He was the President of the IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Society from 2006 to 2007 and the Editor-in-Chief of the IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON GEOSCIENCE AND REMOTE SENSING (TGARS) from 1996 to 2001. He has been the Chair of PIERS since 2008. He is a member of the US National Academy of Engineering.

**Xiaolan Xu** (Senior Member, IEEE) received the B.Eng. degree from Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China, in 2006, and the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in electrical engineering from the University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA, in 2008 and 2011, respectively.
In 2012, she joined the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA, as a Post-Doctoral Research Associate and later became a Scientist in 2014. Her expertise lies in the fields of applied electromagnetics, electromagnetic wave propagation, and scattering properties from snow-covered terrain, vegetated land surface, and bare soil. She specialized in the development of forward modeling and retrieval algorithm with applications to Earth remote sensing from space.
Dr. Xu received the URSI Santimay Basu Award in 2020.****
